note: Content-defined chunk boundaries, pinned across the language boundary (PLAN M0.5 task 5).
A chunk's name is the SHA-256 of its raw bytes, so Go's chunker in internal/notes has to cut
every input exactly where chunkBytes in client/src/core/chunk.ts cuts it. One byte off and the
server and a device store the same note as different chunks, and nothing reports it: both
sides still converge, they just stop deduplicating against each other.
Each language checks the other's output. corpusA is cut by TypeScript and checked by Go;
corpusB is cut by Go and checked by TypeScript. Each side also checks that its own corpus is
still what its code cuts today, and that a corrupted vector fails its check.
An entry describes its input with a generator (see generators) instead of carrying the bytes,
and records the input's SHA-256, so that two generators disagreeing is reported as that and
not as a chunker bug. sizes are explicit: min, avg and max exactly as chunkBytes takes them.
cuts are the end offsets of the chunks, in order; names are the lowercase hex SHA-256 of each
chunk's bytes.
sizesForV1 and isTextPath are written by hand and checked by both languages. The two corpus
sections are written by their generators. Both writers keep the whole file in the format
JSON.stringify(value, null, 2) produces, which the TypeScript test checks, so regenerating one
half never shows up as a change to the other.

generators.sha256-ctr: SHA-256(utf8(seed) || counter as a 32-bit big-endian integer) for counter 0, 1, 2, ..., concatenated and truncated to length bytes.
generators.repeat: utf8(text), or the bytes hex spells, repeated and truncated to length bytes. Truncation may cut a character.
generators.mixed: Draws from pieces until at least length bytes are written, then truncates to length. Each draw reads the next two bytes of the sha256-ctr stream for seed as a big-endian 16-bit integer v and appends utf8(pieces[v % pieces.length]).

entries.name: a-empty
entries.why: No bytes and no chunks: a file has chunks if and only if it has content.

entries.name: a-one-byte
entries.why: One byte, one chunk.

entries.name: a-window-minus-one
entries.why: One byte short of a full window, at text sizes: the remainder is the only chunk.

entries.name: a-window
entries.why: Exactly one window.

entries.name: a-window-plus-one
entries.why: One byte past a window, the first byte that rolls.

entries.name: a-fill-phase-only
entries.why: A maximum under the window, so every cut is decided while the hash is still filling and it never rolls.

entries.name: a-window-edge
entries.why: Boundaries tested at 48 bytes, the last unrolled hash, and from 49, the first rolled one.

entries.name: a-rewind-retests-carried-bytes
entries.why: A minimum under four with dense multi-byte text: bytes a trim gives back are hashed again, and tested again, as the next chunk opens.

entries.name: a-text-floor-sizes
entries.why: Multilingual prose at the floor text sizes, which textSizesFor gives a 20 KB note.

entries.name: a-text-scaled-1536
entries.why: Text sizes scaled to a 40 KB note: an average of 1536, which is not a power of two.

entries.name: a-text-scaled-3072
entries.why: Text sizes scaled to a 130 KB note.

entries.name: a-one-long-line

entries.name: a-text-on-the-byte-path

entries.name: a-binary
entries.why: Incompressible bytes at binary sizes.

entries.name: a-at-max-binary

entries.name: a-max-plus-one-binary

entries.name: a-forced-into-4-byte-chars-192
entries.why: Every cut forced, as under a 192-byte ceiling: the first lands one byte into a four-byte character, the rest two.

entries.name: a-forced-into-4-byte-chars-193
entries.why: Every cut forced at 193: the first lands two bytes into a four-byte character, the rest three.

entries.name: a-forced-into-mixed-text
entries.why: Every cut forced at 192 through multilingual text, landing in characters of every width.

entries.name: a-remainder-ends-mid-character
entries.why: The input ends one byte into a three-byte character. The last chunk is the remainder and is never trimmed.

entries.name: a-malformed-continuation-run
entries.why: Nothing but continuation bytes on the UTF-8 path: no lead byte in sight, so nothing is ever trimmed.

entries.name: a-malformed-truncated-leads
entries.why: Four-byte leads promising more than follows, back to back.

entries.name: a-malformed-every-byte
entries.why: Every byte value in turn, which is every malformed shape there is.

entries.name: a-malformed-lead-classes
entries.why: Overlong leads, 0xF5 read as a four-byte lead, 0xF8 and 0xFF read as single bytes, an encoded surrogate: classified as chunk.ts classifies them.

note: Chunk sizes under the protocol 1 rule, which Go's SizesFor implements.
base is textSizesFor(size) for text below TEXT_AS_BINARY_ABOVE (4 MiB), otherwise BINARY_SIZES.
max = min(base.max, serverChunkMax), with nothing reserved below the ceiling: chunkMax bounds
raw bytes, and a body frame's marker byte sits on top of it (plan/protocol.md, Chunk bodies).
max is then raised to at least WINDOW * 4 = 192, and min and avg are clamped to max. A
serverChunkMax of 0 or less means the server has not said, and stands for BINARY_SIZES.max.
TypeScript's sizesFor still subtracts SEAL_OVERHEAD, because the client stays end-to-end
encrypted until the M2 strip and changing its ceiling before then would break it. Until then
its test checks these cases against sizesFor with the overhead handed back; PLAN M2 task 2
removes the overhead and checks sizesFor against them directly.
The expected values were computed from this statement of the rule, not from either
implementation.

text at 50176 bytes: the quotient is exactly 3.5 and rounds up
text at 1 MiB scales to an 8 KiB average
text one byte under the binary threshold is still text
text at exactly the threshold is chunked as binary
a 1 GiB text file is chunked as binary
binary at the default ceiling keeps the whole MiB, with nothing reserved
a small binary file still takes binary sizes

a negative ceiling means the server has not said
a ceiling larger than the table maximum is not reached for
a ceiling below the binary maximum becomes the maximum
a ceiling below the binary average clamps the average
a ceiling below the binary minimum clamps all three
a text ceiling exactly at the table maximum is not reduced
a text ceiling one under the table maximum

a ceiling of 191 is raised to 192

note: Whether a path is chunked as text: looksLikeText in chunk.ts, IsTextPath in internal/notes.
The extension is everything after the last dot anywhere in the path, lowercased, and looked
up in textExtensions. Go lowercases ASCII only, which agrees with toLowerCase on every path
these extensions can match. strings.ToLower would not: it maps U+0130 to a plain i, which the
refs.BİB case catches. textExtensions is the whole list, and both sides compare their own
list against it, so an extension added on one side only fails a test.
